                                                                                                                                        337   Our review is limited by the number of studies (N=13) and heterogeneous methods across original

                                                                                                                                        338   studies, hampering a quantitative analysis of the incidence of acute hamstring injuries in soccer. This




Downloaded from www.jospt.org at Ohio State University on December 15, 2020. For personal use only. No other uses without permission.
                                                                                                                                        339   is an example that underpins the importance of common methodologies and clear definitions. In

                                                                                                                                        340   attempt to raise the inclusion rate, authors of eligible studies with missing data, e.g. exposure hours,

                                                                                                                                        341   were contacted by email. With a low response rate and lack of registration of exposure hours, the

                                                                                                                                        342   majority of these studies were excluded.


                                                                                                                                        343   We excluded retrospective studies, limiting the amount of data. Excluding retrospective designs




Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
                                                                                                                                        344   minimizes risk of bias, and it adheres to a consensus statement for the prospective data collection in

                                                                                                                                        345   soccer.12


                                                                                                                                        346   Unpublished data on injury surveillance could be missing. Professional teams and leagues often

                                                                                                                                        347   register injury data without the intention to publish these data. It is unknown how many teams keep

                                                                                                                                        348   these registrations, and we have not searched for these data (grey literature).


                                                                                                                                        349


                                                                                                                                        350   Five recommendations for future research



                                                                                                                                                                                                  16
                                                                                                                                         351   Observations from this systematic review stress the importance of a standardized approach to

                                                                                                                                        352   assessing the incidence of acute hamstring injuries.


                                                                                                                                        353   Recommendation 1: Clear definition of all aspects of the studied injury, such as character (acute or

                                                                                                                                        354   non-acute) should be the foundation of thorough research.


                                                                                                                                        355   Recommendation 2: A standardized approach is essential for registering exposure hours. We excluded

                                                                                                                                        356   studies using Athlete Exposure. This incidence measure counts individual sessions as opposed to

                                                                                                                                        357   accounting for the true exposure. For example, one session of training is ‘1’ Athlete Exposure,




Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
                                                                                                                                        358   however this could be 0.5 or 2 exposure hours. To facilitate comparison and review of literature, it is

                                                                                                                                        359   essential that the field uses the same methodologies, including recording exposure in minutes.12


                                                                                                                                        360   Recommendation 3: Document exposure hours and specify injuries to the muscle group level. A large

                                                                                                                                        361   number of hamstring injuries are registered using the generic term ‘thigh’ injuries. With other thigh

                                                                                                                                        362   injuries, like quadriceps injuries, these data are useless for research on hamstring injuries. We

                                                                                                                                        363   excluded 51 studies because of missing data on exposure hours and the absence of specific numbers




Downloaded from www.jospt.org at Ohio State University on December 15, 2020. For personal use only. No other uses without permission.
                                                                                                                                        364   for hamstring injuries.


                                                                                                                                        365   Recommendation 4: Intensity of play should be taken into account when expressing incidence of acute

                                                                                                                                        366   hamstring injuries. The validity of expressing exposure in ‘hours’ for the incidence of acute hamstring

                                                                                                                                        367   injuries has been questioned recently.18 Acute hamstring injuries occur with rapid eccentric loading

                                                                                                                                        368   and might be less related to amount of exposure hours and more to intensity of play. 21 Using modern




Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
                                                                                                                                        369   registration methods, these activities can be monitored. Many different electronic tracking systems are

                                                                                                                                        370   available (e.g. GPS trackers, motion sensors and video analytics). Technology is rapidly evolving and

                                                                                                                                        371   all of these have different strengths and limitations, with no current gold standard.


                                                                                                                                        372   Recommendation 5: Acute hamstring injuries in female soccer players warrant further investigation.

                                                                                                                                        373   Only two of the included studies included female players. With the growing popularity of soccer

                                                                                                                                        374   among women11, this is a field worthy of study.


                                                                                                                                        375



                                                                                                                                                                                                  17
                                                                                                                                         376   Conclusions


                                                                                                                                        377   The incidence rate of acute hamstring injuries in training and matches ranged from 0.3 to 1.9 injuries

                                                                                                                                        378   per 1000 exposure hours. Acute hamstring injuries accounted for 5% to 13% of all injuries in soccer.

                                                                                                                                        379   The rate of hamstring injury recurrence was 4% to 68% and should be cautiously interpreted.


                                                                                                                                        380   The strength of the evidence was limited by a lack of methodological rigor, the use of varying

                                                                                                                                        381   definitions for acute hamstring injuries, and a heterogeneous conduct of studies on acute hamstring

                                                                                                                                        382   injuries.

                                                                                                                                        396   Findings


                                                                                                                                        397   The incidence of acute hamstring injuries in training and matches was 0.3 to 1.9 injuries per 1000

                                                                                                                                        398   exposure hours. Acute hamstring injuries accounted for 5% to 13% of all soccer injuries.

                                                                                                                                        401   Knowledge of the incidence of acute hamstring injuries in soccer contributes to quantifying its burden

                                                                                                                                        402   and may facilitate the prevention of hamstring injuries by increasing awareness with players, clubs and

                                                                                                                                        403   coaches.

212	               Introduction
213	5
214	6              Strength training is an important component of training in most sports as well as in the area of
215	7
216	8
217	               injury prevention and rehabilitation (Escamilla & Wickham, 2003). In the prescription of
218	9
219	10
220	11             resistance exercise, training intensity or the load used is commonly regarded as the most
221	12
222	13             important variable (Fleck & Kraemer, 1997). The intensity in dynamic resistance training is
223	14
224	15
225	16             often quantified as a function of the maximum weight that can be lifted only once (one
226	17
227	18             repetition maximum, 1RM). Most authors agree that the load should be at least 60% of 1RM
228	19
229	20             in order to stimulate increases in strength and that optimal strength gains results from loads in
230	21
231	22
232	23             excess of 80% of 1RM (Atha, 1981; Häkkinen, 1994; Fleck & Kraemer, 1997; ACSM, 2002;
233	24
234	25             Andersen et al, 2006). For muscle hypertrophy, loads of 6-12RM are usually recommended,
235	26
236	27             corresponding to ~70-85% of 1RM (Häkkinen, 1994; Fleck & Kraemer, 1997; ACSM, 2002).
237	
238	
239	                                                PR
240	28
241	29
242	30                   In the clinical setting, however, it is often difficult and sometimes also contraindicated
243	31
244	32             to use near-maximal loads (e.g. early rehabilitation after a sports injury). Muscle atrophy and
245	
246	
247	                                                         OO
248	33
249	34
250	35
251	               weakness often occur rapidly in the affected area due to the effects of trauma (or disease) and
252	36
253	37             inactivity. Consequently, training modalities that promote hypertrophy or counteract atrophy
254	38
255	39
256	40
257	                                                                  F
258	               without the use of heavy loads should be of special interest in the rehabilitation of injuries and
259	41
260	42             some chronic diseases for which high musculoskeletal forces are contraindicated.
261	43
262	44                   In the mid 1990’s, Rooney et al. (1994) and Schott et al. (1995) suggested that fatigue
263	45
264	46             and metabolite accumulation were important factors in the resistance exercise stimulus
265	47
266	48
267	49             leading to increased strength and accretion of muscle mass. These findings were extended by
268	50
269	51             Shinohara et al. (1998) and Takarada et al. (2000b), who used tourniquet cuffs to partially
270	52
271	53             restrict the muscle blood flow during training with low resistance in order to cause increases
272	54
273	55
274	56             in muscle strength. In these and in several subsequent studies (Takarada et al., 2002, 2004;
275	57
276	58             Burgomaster et al., 2003; Abe et al, 2005a, b; Kubo et al., 2006) low to moderate intensity
277	59
278	60
279	               (20-50% of 1RM) resistance training with vascular occlusion has been shown to lead to gains

294	7
295	8    training with tourniquets (Abe et al., 2006). It has also been reported that brief intermittent
296	9
297	10
298	     tourniquet-induced ischemia-reperfusion, without exercise, can decrease disuse atrophy; at
299	11

308	19

312	23

340	     It is generally believed that only muscle fibers that are activated during exercise grow as a
341	43
342	44   result of strength training (Kraemer, Fleck & Evans, 1996). The size principle of motor unit
343	45
344	46   recruitment dictates that small units composed of slow but fatigue resistant fibers are recruited
345	47
346	48
347	49   first and with increasing demands for force or power, ever larger units are recruited
348	50
349	51   (Henneman et al., 1965). Studies using glycogen depletion (Gollnick et al., 1974a, b;
350	52
351	53   Vøllestad et al., 1984, 1985) and alterations in phosphocreatine-to-creatine ratios in muscle
352	54
353	55
354	56   fibers (Beltman et al., 2004a, b) have supported the notion that the size principle is operating
355	57
356	58   in humans during exercise. Thus, units with type I fibers are usually recruited first and with
357	59
358	60   increasing intensity of exercise, units comprised of type IIa fibers and finally also units with
359

387	19

 "id":"Q17",
 "sourceFile":"Focused review of sleep wearable technology and its application in sports performance.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",

 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"The PDF title 'Focused Review of Sleep Wearable Technology and Its Application in Sports Performance' and the six listed authors match the filename and the Crossref title.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain":"Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains":["Monitoring & Technology","Recovery & Readiness"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Research & Analytics","Coaching"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Narrative review of actigraphy and consumer sleep wearable studies in athletes and non-athletes, which the authors state is more narrative than structured. Wearables detect sleep reasonably well but are weaker at detecting wake, with wake accuracy of about 49% to 60% in validation studies. The authors report that proprietary summary sleep scores have no identified link to training, performance or recovery.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The review describes no search or selection method and presents no new data. Most validation work is industry sponsored, and few studies are athlete-specific, so the review cannot show whether wearable sleep data change performance or recovery outcomes.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read a consumer sleep score as a validated measure of recovery, when the authors state its clinical meaning is unknown.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2025,
   "citation":"Kaufman MW, Shetty M, Nguyen C, Abas J, Fredericson M, Zeitzer J. Focused Review of Sleep Wearable Technology and Its Application in Sports Performance. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2025;24(6):171-176.",
   "doi":"10.1249/jsr.0000000000001258",
   "abstract":"The authors review the history, accuracy and current use of sleep wearables, which are mostly wrist-worn actigraphs. They conclude that wearables detect sleep reasonably well but struggle to separate quiet wakefulness from early sleep, and that proprietary sleep scores are not yet clinically interpretable for athletes.",
   "tldr":"Sleep wearables can show sleep trends across a season, but their summary scores have not been linked to training, performance or recovery. When the device and the athlete's own sense of sleep disagree, the athlete's report should take priority.",
   "methods":"Narrative review of published actigraphy validation studies and athlete sleep studies. The authors state the review is more narrative than structured because device validity depends on hardware and software that can change.",
   "findings":"Wearables show high sensitivity for sleep but poor specificity for wake, with wake accuracy of about 49% to 60% in validation studies. Actigraphy agreed with polysomnography at 81% to 90% in elite athletes in the cited work. No study has linked a consumer summary sleep score to training, performance or recovery outcomes.",
   "limitations":"The authors acknowledge that the review is not structured, that many validation studies are industry sponsored, and that device algorithms are proprietary. The paper presents no original data.",
   "practicalImplications":"Use wearables to see sleep trends across a season and around travel or schedule changes, but do not treat a summary sleep score as a clinical result. Keep clinical presentation and subjective report as the basis for decisions.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: track sleep trends across a season, including travel, to see how schedule changes line up with training and recovery. Do not set sleep-score targets for athletes, since the score's link to performance is unestablished.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: the review suggests wearables may help detect sleep disturbances that can accompany concussion, but it states they are not sensitive or specific enough to diagnose or clear an athlete. Clinical examination and the athlete's report should guide decisions."
 }
}

 "id":"Q19",
 "sourceFile":"How Do They Decide - Performance Support Staff Perceptions of Decision-Making in Elite-Sport Environments.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"The PDF title 'How Do They Decide? Performance Support Staff Perceptions of Decision-Making in Elite-Sport Environments' and the authors Wilson, Roe and Kiely match the filename and the Crossref title.",
 "confidence":"medium",
 "studyDesign":"Cross-sectional Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Training & Performance",
 "domains":["Training & Performance","Brain Health & Psychology"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Coaching","Sports Medicine","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Professional / Elite"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Online mixed-methods survey of 191 performance support staff (179 men, 12 women) working in professional or international sport, recruited by social media and referral. Most rated decision-making as very important (98% scored 5 or higher on a 7-point scale), but only 31% had formal decision-making training, 69% had no formal strategy for scoring key decisions, and 22% consistently reviewed and updated plans. Thematic analysis of open responses identified environmental pressures, lack of systems, underdeveloped decision skills, dysfunctional team dynamics and cognitive biases as obstacles.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Nonprobability recruitment from the authors' networks and a sample that is 94% male limit generalizability, and the findings describe staff perceptions rather than measured decision quality or athlete outcomes. The sample is staff rather than athletes, so the Professional / Elite tag describes the sport context, and the primary domain is Training & Performance because decision-making in performance support is the main subject.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the survey percentages as a measure of how common poor decision-making is across elite sport, when this was a self-selected sample of mostly men recruited through the authors' networks.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2024,
   "citation":"Wilson PJ, Roe G, Kiely J. How Do They Decide? Performance Support Staff Perceptions of Decision-Making in Elite-Sport Environments. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2024.",
   "doi":"10.1519/jsc.0000000000004989",
   "abstract":"A mixed-methods online survey of 191 performance support staff in professional or international sport examined their views on decision-making, how they learn it and how they track decisions. Most rated decision-making as very important, but few had formal training or a formal review process, and staff described pressure, poor team communication and cognitive biases as obstacles.",
   "tldr":"Performance staff rate decision-making as central to their role, yet most have no formal training and no structured way to review key decisions. The authors suggest starting with basic education on decision-making and cognitive bias, then adding a formal process for tracking and reviewing major decisions.",
   "methods":"Nonprobability (purposive and snowball) recruitment over an 8-week period. An online questionnaire with nine decision-making items (eight closed, one open) and six demographic items was checked by a five-expert panel. Closed items were summarized descriptively, and the open item was analysed by thematic analysis.",
   "findings":"Decision-making was rated 5 or higher by 98% of respondents (median 7). Ninety percent believed team decisions give better outcomes than individual decisions. Thirty-one percent had received formal decision-making education, 69% had no formal strategy for scoring key decisions, and 22% consistently reviewed and adjusted plans. Five themes emerged from the open responses: environmental pressures, lack of systems and processes, underdeveloped decision capabilities, dysfunctional team dynamics and cognitive biases.",
   "limitations":"The authors note that the sample was recruited non-randomly, that only 12 respondents were women, and that the findings may not generalize to all professional sport. The survey did not measure the type of decision training received, and the preference for experiential over targeted training (median 3 on a 7-point scale) was not explored further. The PDF is dated 2024 while Crossref lists 2025, and the PDF year is used.",
   "practicalImplications":"Organizations can start with basic education on decision-making and cognitive bias, then add a formal process for recording and reviewing major decisions. Team decision-making depends on trust and communication, which respondents named as barriers.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: staff who make training-load, selection or return-related calls can keep a simple log of key decisions and their outcomes and review it on a set schedule. The paper does not test whether this improves decision quality.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: the study does not test return-to-play decisions, but respondents described conflicts over return from injury around key games. Use the findings to review how return decisions are made and who is involved, not as evidence for a specific return protocol."
 }
}

{
 "id":"Q21",
 "sourceFile":"Incidence of acute hamstring injuries in soccer - A systematic review of 13 studies involving more than 3800 athletes with 2 million sport exposure hours.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"The PDF title 'Incidence of acute hamstring injuries in soccer: A systematic review of 13 studies involving more than 3800 athletes with 2 million sport exposure hours' (Diemer et al.) matches the filename and the Crossref title.",
 "confidence":"medium",
 "studyDesign":"Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Monitoring & Technology"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Rehabilitation","Research & Analytics","Coaching"],
 "sports":["Soccer"],
 "populations":["Professional / Elite","Adult / Recreational","Male Athletes","Female Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42016039011) of prospective studies in adult soccer players reporting acute hamstring injuries per 1000 exposure hours. Thirteen studies with 3868 players and about 2.07 million exposure hours were included, and the synthesis was descriptive because definitions and exposure recording differed. The authors report 0.3 to 1.9 acute hamstring injuries per 1000 exposure hours, recurrence of 4% to 68%, and certainty of evidence from moderate to very low.",
 "screeningLimitations":"No pooled estimate was calculated, only two included studies reported women, and 51 studies were excluded for missing exposure hours or hamstring-specific counts. The findings therefore describe a narrow evidence base with heterogeneous injury definitions.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could compare these incidence figures directly with their own squad's injury rates, when the included studies used different injury definitions and exposure measures.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2021,
   "citation":"Diemer WM, Winters M, Tol JL, Pas HIMFL, Moen MH. Incidence of acute hamstring injuries in soccer: a systematic review of 13 studies involving more than 3800 athletes with 2 million sport exposure hours. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2021.",
   "doi":"10.2519/jospt.2021.9305",
   "abstract":"Thirteen prospective studies of adult soccer players were summarized descriptively to estimate acute hamstring injury incidence and recurrence. Incidence was 0.3 to 1.9 per 1000 exposure hours, and recurrence ranged from 4% to 68%, with certainty of evidence rated from moderate to very low.",
   "tldr":"Acute hamstring injuries in soccer occur at roughly 0.3 to 1.9 per 1000 exposure hours in training and matches. The wide range reflects inconsistent injury definitions and exposure recording, so compare your own data with these figures only after matching definitions.",
   "methods":"PRISMA-guided systematic review, prospectively registered in PROSPERO. Five databases were searched to August 2019 without language or date limits, and two reviewers screened and extracted data. Eligible studies were prospective, in adult soccer players, and reported acute hamstring injuries with exposure hours. Quality was assessed with a modified Newcastle-Ottawa scale and certainty with GRADE.",
   "findings":"Incidence was 0.4 to 1.9 per 1000 hours with time-loss definitions and 0.3 to 1.0 with tissue-based definitions. Professional players had 0.5 to 1.9 per 1000 hours with time-loss definitions, and women in two studies had 0.3 to 0.5. Acute hamstring injuries made up 5% to 15% of all soccer injuries across seven studies, and recurrence ranged from 4% to 68% depending on the definition and follow-up window. Certainty was very low for most measures.",
   "limitations":"The authors note the small number of studies, heterogeneous methods, exclusion of studies without exposure hours, and very low certainty for most measures. The PDF text carries no printed publication year (the copyright line is an unfilled template and the December 2020 stamp is a download date), so the year 2021 is taken from Crossref. The abstract and results give 5% to 15% of injuries while the Conclusions and Key Points give 5% to 13%, and the record uses the results value.",
   "practicalImplications":"Use the 0.3 to 1.9 per 1000 hour range as a rough benchmark for how common acute hamstring injuries are in soccer. Record exposure hours in minutes and classify injuries by muscle group and by time loss, so that your own surveillance can be compared with published rates.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: the review gives no training intervention. Its use for performance staff is to set up injury surveillance with exposure hours, muscle-specific injury definitions and, where possible, intensity measures, so that squad data can be compared later.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: the review does not set return-to-play timelines. It reports recurrence of 4% to 68% and notes that recurrence definitions drive those rates, so the figures should be interpreted cautiously and not used alone for return decisions."
 }
}

 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Consensus / Position Statement",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Rehabilitation","Performance"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Consensus statement from the Team Physician Consensus Conference, a six-organization project, written by 14 authors for team physicians caring for athletes from youth to Olympic level. It covers initial assessment and management of shoulder dislocation, the disabled throwing shoulder, ulnar collateral ligament tear, hamstring injury, ACL tear, meniscus tear, ankle sprain, groin pain and femoroacetabular impingement, and hip and groin apophyseal injury, using essential and desirable statements. The authors state that nonoperative care is the usual first step for most of these injuries and that multimodal prevention programs reduce ACL and hamstring injury incidence.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The statement is explicitly not a standard of care, applies no systematic review, and gives no evidence levels or recommendation grades. It covers only select injuries, so many common presentations are outside its scope.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could treat these statements as a standard of care or as graded recommendations, when the authors say neither applies.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2024,
   "citation":"Herring SA, Kibler WB, Putukian M, Boyajian-O'Neill LA, Chang CJ, Franks RR, et al. Initial Assessment and Management of Select Musculoskeletal Injuries: A Team Physician Consensus Statement. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2024;23(3):86-104.",
   "doi":"10.1249/jsr.0000000000001151",
   "abstract":"The Team Physician Consensus Conference summarizes initial assessment and management of select musculoskeletal injuries in athletes. Each topic covers mechanism, clinical presentation, evaluation, nonoperative and operative options and injury risk modification, with statements labelled essential or desirable.",
   "tldr":"This is a practical reference for the first assessment and early management of shoulder dislocation, UCL, hamstring, ACL, meniscus, ankle, groin and apophyseal injuries. It is a consensus guide rather than a graded evidence review, so check specific decisions against current literature.",
   "methods":"Expert consensus. An executive committee selected topics and drafted an outline, representatives of six professional organizations reviewed the literature for each topic, and statements were agreed by unanimous consensus at in-person meetings before board approval. The statement was co-published in Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise (2024;56(3):385-401). No systematic review, levels of evidence or recommendation grades were included.",
   "findings":"Each topic lists essential information every team physician should know and desirable information for ideal settings. Nonoperative care is the initial approach for most disabled throwing shoulder and UCL presentations and most hamstring injuries, with surgery reserved for failed or high-demand cases. The statement reports that multimodal prevention programs reduce ACL and hamstring injury, that eccentric strength training reduces hamstring injury risk, and that core stabilizing exercise reduces load and injury risk.",
   "limitations":"The authors state that the statement is not a standard of care and is general in nature, that only select topics are included, and that no systematic review or evidence grading was done. Several sections note limited high-quality evidence, including for biologic and corticosteroid injections, stretching as a risk modifier, and the value of biologic therapy for UCL injury.",
   "practicalImplications":"Use the essential points as a first-assessment checklist: confirm the mechanism, examine neurovascular status, obtain the imaging named for each injury, and set referral criteria. Treat the surgical indications as triggers for referral rather than default plans.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: the workload and kinetic-chain sections, which cover monitoring load and screening the whole kinetic chain for throwing shoulder and UCL injury, can guide load planning for throwers. The statement names eccentric strength and core work as the main hamstring risk-modification items.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: the statement treats return to play as an individualized decision. It says most athletes out of overhead sport after UCL reconstruction are out for 12 months or longer and that throwers need a specific throwing protocol before return. It does not give return timelines for most injuries, so use the injury-specific criteria in the full text."
 }
}

 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Consensus statement from the Team Physician Consensus Conference, a six-organization project, written by 14 authors for team physicians caring for athletes from youth to Olympic level. It covers initial assessment and management of shoulder dislocation, the disabled throwing shoulder, ulnar collateral ligament tear, hamstring injury, ACL tear, meniscus tear, ankle sprain, groin pain and femoroacetabular impingement, and hip and groin apophyseal injury, using essential and desirable statements. The authors state that nonoperative care is the usual first step for most of these injuries and that multimodal prevention programs reduce ACL and hamstring injury incidence.",

 "paper":{
   "year":2024,
   "citation":"Herring SA, Kibler WB, Putukian M, Boyajian-O'Neill LA, Chang CJ, Franks RR, et al. Initial Assessment and Management of Select Musculoskeletal Injuries: A Team Physician Consensus Statement. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2024;23(3):86-104.",
   "doi":"10.1249/jsr.0000000000001151",
   "abstract":"The Team Physician Consensus Conference summarizes initial assessment and management of select musculoskeletal injuries in athletes. Each topic covers mechanism, clinical presentation, evaluation, nonoperative and operative options and injury risk modification, with statements labelled essential or desirable.",
   "tldr":"This is a practical reference for the first assessment and early management of shoulder dislocation, UCL, hamstring, ACL, meniscus, ankle, groin and apophyseal injuries. It is a consensus guide rather than a graded evidence review, so check specific decisions against current literature.",
   "methods":"Expert consensus. An executive committee selected topics and drafted an outline, representatives of six professional organizations reviewed the literature for each topic, and statements were agreed by unanimous consensus at in-person meetings before board approval. The statement was co-published in Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise (2024;56(3):385-401). No systematic review, levels of evidence or recommendation grades were included.",
   "findings":"Each topic lists essential information every team physician should know and desirable information for ideal settings. Nonoperative care is the initial approach for most disabled throwing shoulder and UCL presentations and most hamstring injuries, with surgery reserved for failed or high-demand cases. The statement reports that multimodal prevention programs reduce ACL and hamstring injury, that eccentric strength training reduces hamstring injury risk, and that core stabilizing exercise reduces load and injury risk.",
   "limitations":"The authors state that the statement is not a standard of care and is general in nature, that only select topics are included, and that no systematic review or evidence grading was done. Several sections note limited high-quality evidence, including for biologic and corticosteroid injections, stretching as a risk modifier, and the value of biologic therapy for UCL injury.",
   "practicalImplications":"Use the essential points as a first-assessment checklist: confirm the mechanism, examine neurovascular status, obtain the imaging named for each injury, and set referral criteria. Treat the surgical indications as triggers for referral rather than default plans.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: the workload and kinetic-chain sections, which cover monitoring load and screening the whole kinetic chain for throwing shoulder and UCL injury, can guide load planning for throwers. The statement names eccentric strength and core work as the main hamstring risk-modification items.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: the statement treats return to play as an individualized decision. It says most athletes out of overhead sport after UCL reconstruction are out for 12 months or longer and that throwers need a specific throwing protocol before return. It does not give return timelines for most injuries, so use the injury-specific criteria in the full text."
 }
}

{
 "id":"Q23",
 "sourceFile":"Intermittent Fasting and Its    Effects on Athletic Performance- A Review.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"The PDF title 'Intermittent Fasting and Its Effects on Athletic Performance: A Review' (Levy and Chu) matches the filename and the Crossref title.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain":"Nutrition & Hydration",
 "domains":["Nutrition & Hydration","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Nutrition","Sports Medicine","Performance","Athletic Training"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Narrative review of studies of intermittent fasting, including Ramadan fasting, time-restricted eating and alternate-day fasting, across high-intensity, endurance and resistance exercise. Most cited studies are small crossover or observational studies in footballers, cyclists, rowers or resistance-trained men, plus one mouse study. The authors report mixed results, with some studies showing reduced sprint, cycling, rowing or endurance performance and others showing no effect, and no study showing a performance benefit.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The review describes no search strategy or inclusion criteria, and its evidence is mostly small studies and Ramadan fasting, which also changes sleep and fluid intake. The authors also define the 5:2 diet inconsistently between the Introduction (alternating days) and the Discussion (5 days fasting, 2 days eating).",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read 'no benefit' as proof that intermittent fasting harms performance, when the authors describe mixed results from mostly small, short-term studies.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2019,
   "citation":"Levy E, Chu T. Intermittent Fasting and Its Effects on Athletic Performance: A Review. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2019;18(7):266-269.",
   "doi":"10.1249/jsr.0000000000000614",
   "abstract":"The authors review studies on intermittent fasting and athletic performance across high-intensity, endurance and resistance exercise. Most data come from Ramadan fasting and overnight fasts. They report varied outcomes, with no study showing an improvement in performance, and call for long-term studies of specific fasting protocols.",
   "tldr":"Intermittent fasting does not appear to improve athletic performance and may impair sprint, cycling, rowing or endurance output in some studies. Athletes who fast should track their performance on fasting and fed days, and current data do not support fasting as a rapid weight-loss method before weigh-ins.",
   "methods":"Narrative review of published studies, grouped by exercise type (high-intensity, endurance and resistance) and by fasting type (Ramadan, time-restricted and alternate-day). The authors cite a 2018 systematic review of fasted-state exercise, but no search method or selection criteria are described for this review.",
   "findings":"In Ramadan studies, several showed small, non-significant decreases in sprint performance, and one study of Algerian footballers reported a 16% decrease in endurance capacity. In a 2019 crossover study of ten rowers, omitting breakfast impaired evening 2000 m time-trial performance, and cyclists who skipped breakfast had lower evening performance. Resistance training studies over 8 weeks found little or no harm to lean mass or strength, although one reported lower testosterone and IGF-1 at 8 weeks.",
   "limitations":"The authors note varied definitions of fasting, varied outcome measures, small samples, and few studies of the specific 5:2 and 16:8 regimens. Ramadan studies confound fasting with sleep disruption and dehydration, and the mouse work may not transfer to humans.",
   "practicalImplications":"Athletes who adopt intermittent fasting should track sprint, cycling or time-trial output on fasting and fed days, because impairments appeared in several studies. Coaches should not expect intermittent fasting to improve performance, and current data do not support its use for rapid weight loss in weight-class sports.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: if an athlete fasts, log high-intensity and endurance output across fasting and fed days, since the review found impairments and no benefit. Resistance training appeared less affected, though the studies were short.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: the review does not address injury or return to sport and cannot inform return-to-play decisions."
 }
}

{
 "id":"Q24",
 "sourceFile":"Ischemic strength training - a low load alternative to heavy resistance exercise .pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"The PDF title 'Ischemic Strength Training: A Low-Load Alternative to Heavy Resistance Exercise?' (Wernbom, Augustsson and Raastad, Scandinavian Journal of Medicine and Science in Sports proof) matches the filename and the Crossref title.",
 "confidence":"medium",
 "studyDesign":"Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain":"Training & Performance",
 "domains":["Training & Performance","Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Rehabilitation","Athletic Training","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Narrative review of strength training combined with vascular occlusion (ischemic or Kaatsu training), covering motor unit recruitment, hormones, growth factors, safety, cuff width and dose. The authors cite 13 training studies with 116 subjects, mostly untrained or physically active adults, in which low-load training with a cuff produced strength and muscle size gains comparable to heavy training in several studies. They conclude the method appears relatively safe in the short term, but the mechanisms are unclear and tendon and possibly neural adaptations appear smaller than with heavy training.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The review states it summarizes current opinion and describes no search method, so study selection cannot be reproduced. Most evidence comes from 2 to 8 week studies, with two of 16 weeks, and much of the safety data comes from a national survey published by the same research group.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could assume that low-load cuff training matches heavy lifting for every goal, when the paper reports smaller tendon and possibly neural effects and most gains came from sets taken to or near failure.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2008,
   "citation":"Wernbom M, Augustsson J, Raastad T. Ischemic Strength Training: A Low-Load Alternative to Heavy Resistance Exercise? Scandinavian Journal of Medicine and Science in Sports. 2008.",
   "doi":"10.1111/j.1600-0838.2008.00788.x",
   "abstract":"The authors review the physiology, safety and dosing of strength training combined with vascular occlusion. They note that low-load occlusion training produces strength and size gains comparable to heavy training in several studies, but that mechanisms, long-term safety and practical use remain unclear. They suggest that relative ischemia may occur without a cuff at some loads.",
   "tldr":"Low-load training with a tourniquet can build muscle and strength, but the mechanisms, long-term safety and practical dose are unresolved. Where heavy loads are contraindicated, it is an option, with wide cuffs at lower pressures preferred and attention to soreness and effort.",
   "methods":"Narrative review of the authors' and published work on motor unit recruitment, hormonal and local growth factor responses, safety, cuff width and training dose. The authors summarize 13 training studies in Table 1, but no search strategy or inclusion criteria are described.",
   "findings":"Low-load training with partial occlusion at about 20% to 50% of 1RM produced muscle size and strength gains comparable to heavy training in several studies. In one study, a low-load occlusion leg and a high-load leg gained similar quadriceps volume, but only the high-load leg increased tendon-aponeurosis stiffness. A Japanese survey of more than 12,600 occlusion-training users reported subcutaneous hemorrhage in 13.1% and rare serious events, including venous thrombosis in 0.055%.",
   "limitations":"The authors state that long-term safety, soft-tissue effects, optimal frequency and whether cuffs add benefit beyond effort need further study. Several supporting points rest on unpublished observations, and one partial-occlusion cycling study (Eiken et al.) found an 8% fall in peak torque despite fiber-area gains.",
   "practicalImplications":"If a cuff is used, the authors favor relatively wide cuffs at lower pressures, noting about 90 to 110 mm Hg was enough in their unpublished observations, rather than high pressures with narrow cuffs. Expect intense muscle pain and delayed soreness, which the authors say lessens with low starting volumes of 1 to 2 sets, and note that the training demands high motivation.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: the review supports low-load occlusion as a complement to strength work or when heavy loads are inappropriate. It does not show it beats heavy training for tendon or neural adaptation, so do not use it to replace heavy lifting for strength-focused athletes.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: the review is aimed at rehabilitation where heavy forces are contraindicated, but it gives no return-to-play criteria and no injured-athlete trials. Any use should be under clinical oversight, since the authors call soft-tissue and safety effects unresolved."
 }
}
